channel.title: Custom Tire & Industrial Labels Resources
channel.description: Buyer guides for custom tire labels, industrial labels, barcode labels and label material selection.

item.title: Tire Sidewall vs Tread Barcode Labels: Choose the Scan Surface
item.description: The same SKU can look perfectly readable on a proof and disappear once the tire is stacked. Choose sidewall or tread only after watching where a worker actually sees, applies and scans the label.

item.title: Tire Label Roll Changeover: Keep Adjacent Sizes and Revisions Apart
item.description: Two rolls can share the same color and almost the same tire size. At changeover, the question is not whether the artwork looks familiar; it is whether the roll, job ticket and first applied label agree.

item.title: Labels on Anodized Aluminum Equipment: Finish, Cleaning and Proof
item.description: A smooth-looking aluminum sample is not the whole job. The approved label needs to meet the exact anodized finish, cleaning routine, placement and data that operators will handle.

item.title: Asset ID Labels on Removable Machine Guards: Keep IDs With the Right Part
item.description: When a machine guard comes off for service, a label placed only on that guard may travel with the panel. Keep the permanent machine ID and the removable part ID distinct, and do not cover safety information.

item.title: Warehouse Rack-Beam Barcode Labels: Location ID, Not Product ID
item.description: The rack position stays when its contents change. A location label should answer where to put or pick an item, not pretend to identify whichever carton happens to sit above it today.

item.title: Direct Thermal vs Thermal Transfer Labels: Buy for the Life of the ID
item.description: A carton moving out this week and a pump expected to keep its ID for years should not automatically use the same print system. Start with the job and exposure, then select the printer, face stock and ribbon together.

item.title: Tire Pallet Labels After Stretch Wrap: Make the Load Scannable
item.description: A tread label can identify a tire before the load is wrapped. Once film and straps cover the stack, the receiving dock may need a separate outer pallet identifier. Plan that scan point before the wrapping station.

item.title: Secondary Container Workplace Labels: Do Not Copy the Shipping Label Blindly
item.description: A plant transfer bottle is not necessarily labeled under the same rule as a container leaving the supplier. The employer must approve the hazard information and the workplace system before the printer makes the sticker.

item.title: Forklift Asset ID Labels vs Capacity Plates: Know Which One You Are Printing
item.description: A fleet number helps maintenance find a truck. A capacity plate tells an operator what the truck can lift. Put the first where staff can read it without covering, imitating or altering the second.

item.title: Spare Parts Kit Labels vs Component Labels: One Box, Several Identities
item.description: A maintenance kit has its own pick and issue task, while the bolts, seals and bearings inside may have separate part numbers. Make the outside label useful without turning a kit number into a substitute for each component.

item.title: RFID vs Printed Tire Labels: Two Different Identification Jobs
item.description: An embedded RFID identifier and a printed tread label can coexist, but they answer different questions. Decide who must identify the tire, where, and with which equipment before ordering either.

item.title: Automatic Tire Label Rolls: The Applicator Needs More Than Artwork
item.description: A beautiful tire label can still stop a line if the liner, gap or winding direction does not suit the machine. Build the roll specification from the actual applicator manual and a line sample.

item.title: Warehouse Bin Labels vs Part Labels: Keep Place and Product Separate
item.description: The bin stays in place while parts move. A location label tells staff where to go; a part label tells them what they have. Printing the same code on both creates quiet inventory errors.

item.title: Barcode Verification vs Scan Test: What Did You Actually Check?
item.description: One scanner reading one sample is useful, but it does not prove every label meets a print-quality standard or that the encoded value is correct. Separate those three checks before approving a run.

item.title: Coastal Equipment ID Labels: Specify Exposure, Not Just Salt Hours
item.description: Near the coast, a sticker faces spray, sunlight, cleaning, temperature swings and a real mounting surface. A single salt-fog number cannot stand in for that whole service environment.

item.title: Tire QR Code or Linear Barcode: Which Scan Job Comes First?
item.description: A camera-friendly code and a warehouse scan code may point to different things. Before choosing a symbol, name the scanner, the data owner and what a successful scan must return.

item.title: Mixed Tire Pallet Labels: One Load, Several SKUs
item.description: A pallet carrying three tire sizes is not one tire SKU. Its outer label should identify the shipping unit and direct the receiver to the approved contents record.

item.title: Pipe Markers vs Valve Tags: What Does Each Need to Say?
item.description: A pipe marker answers what is in the line and where it flows. A valve tag identifies the particular control point. One should not be forced to do the entire job of the other.

item.title: Washdown Equipment ID Labels: Cleaning Is Part of the Specification
item.description: A label that survives a damp room may still fail under repeated spray, heat or cleaner contact. Specify how the equipment is cleaned, not just that it gets wet.

item.title: Reusable Tote Labels: Keep the Container ID, Change the Trip Data
item.description: The tote returns; the shipment changes. Give the container a stable identity, and put route or order information on a separate changeable label.
